short_description: When the 45-year-old Henri Matisse was rejected from military service at the outbreak of World War I, a friend encouraged him to contribute to the war effort the best way he could: by continuing to paint well. This led to a productive period of compositional and material experimentation—including this canvas—that Matisse hoped would sustain the tradition of French painting in the face of a cultural and national threat.

title: Still Life—Strawberries, Nuts, &c.
short_description: During Raphaelle Peale’s time, still lifes were relegated to the bottom of the hierarchy of painting subjects. Peale, however, ignored their low status and is now acknowledged as America’s first professional still-life painter and leading practitioner. In this particularly fine example, the rhythmic balance of fruit, nuts, and Chinese-export porcelain is enlivened by the diagonal branch of grapes becoming raisins and an orange leaf.

title: Portrait of Natalia Goncharova and Mikhail Larionov
The Herring Net
short_description: One of the most influential American painters of the 19th century, Winslow Homer is known for his dynamic depictions of both upper-class leisure pursuits and nature's power and beauty. The paintings he created after 1882 focus almost exclusively on humankind’s contest with nature. Here, Homer depicted the heroic efforts of fishermen hauling in an abundant catch of herring while steadying their boat amid turbulent swells.

title: Tureen
short_description: This exuberant tureen exemplifies the highly imaginative and technically advanced hollowware that made Gorham one of the leading silver manufacturers in the 19th century. The firm was the first major American silver company to introduce Japanese-inspired designs into their product line, ahead of competitors like Tiffany and Company.

title: Couscous Platter
short_description: Female potters of the Aït Bouaddou and other Imazighen groups of Algeria’s mountainous Kabylie region embellish their ceramics for storing, preparing, and serving food with a variety of painted decorations. Drawing on a rich vocabulary of checkerboards, crosses, circles, and triangles, this boldly ornamented platter is enlivened with a symmetrical composition that develops outward from a central point.

title: Still Life with Mouse, New York
Calf's Head and Ox Tongue
short_description: Caillebotte may have been inspired by the butcher’s shop below his family home in Paris when he painted this bloody scene of animal parts ready for human consumption. The painting confronts viewers with objects that are visually unpleasant and yet rendered with highly decorative pastel colors and soft brushstrokes.

title: The Plate of Apples
short_description: In this still life, Paul Cezanne disrupted expectations for painting in the late 1870s by tipping the tabletop and plate forward toward the viewer and constructing a table with edges that don’t quite align. These disorienting details are complemented by the heavy, sculptural forms he created by using a pointed tool to incise contours around the plate and some of the apples.

title: Still Life with Dead Game, Fruits, and Vegetables in a Market
short_description: This overflowing Flemish market stall is enlivened by dead animals splayed on the table, fighting roosters, and a pickpocket. An early example of Frans Snyders’s combination of ornamental still-life elements with secondary figures, this scene might have adorned the dining room of an aristocratic collector. Snyders was the leading Flemish painter of monumental still lifes. He regularly collaborated with his fellow Antwerp artist Peter Paul Rubens.

title: Are They Thinking about the Grape? (Pensent-ils au raisin?)
short_description: This painting is based on a 1745 pantomime about a young shepherd’s awakening love for a shepherdess. The couple feed each other grapes—a fruit associated with Bacchus, god of pleasure—suggesting that their encounter is not entirely chaste. François Boucher’s compositions on pastoral themes are his most influential contribution to 18th-century French art.

title: Fish (Still Life)
short_description: This painting, like many of Manet’s still lifes, recalls 17th-century Dutch models. The directness of execution, bold brushwork, and immediacy of vision, however, suggest why the public found Manet’s work so unorthodox and confrontational. While this painting depicts “dead nature” (nature morte is French for still life), there is nothing still about the work: the produce seems fresh and the handling of the paint vigorous.

title: Stela of Amenemhat and Hemet
date_display: Middle Kingdom, early Dynasty 12, about 1956–1877 BCE
short_description: This vibrantly painted stela commemorates the husband and wife Amenemhat and Hemet in the youthful state they intended to inhabit for eternity. The table piled with food ensures their eternal nourishment and also reflects the practice of family and community members honoring their dead. A stela like this would have been placed in a public location where visitors could come to recite the inscriptions aloud.

title: Apples and Grapes
short_description: Monet probably painted this and other still lifes knowing that they would be more marketable than his landscapes. Here, however, he used the complexity of color, light, and texture found in his most Impressionist landscapes. Particularly evident in the cloth's surface—the light on the horizontal brushstrokes recalls earlier works in which he used similar horizontals of variegated colors to suggest water rippling in the sunlight.

title: Christ Washing the Feet of His Disciples
Relief Fragment Depicting Merettetiiyet with Offerings
date_display: First Intermediate Period, Dynasty 10, about 2050 BCE
short_description: This panel was part of an offering niche designed for a woman named Meret-Teti-iyet. At the top, people bring offerings to sustain her in the afterlife. Below Meret-Teti-iyet faces visitors behind piles of food. On this panel, she holds a closed lotus blossom; on the other panel in our collection, she sniffs an open lotus. The lotus, which opens with the rising sun and sinks beneath the water at night, was a symbol of rebirth in ancient Egypt.

short_description: This is one of a group of related canvases featuring fruit that Van Gogh painted in 1887. In these works, he employed more vibrant colors and used a thicker, broader paint application than he had earlier. Here, he used complementary colors whose contrasting effect is heightened by the pulsating pattern of brushstrokes that defines the tablecloth and creates a force field around the fruit.

title: Foliage—Oak Tree and Fruit Seller
short_description: This large, tapestry-like canvas depicts the lush view from the second-story window of the artist’s vacation home near Versailles, France. Using a limited palette of greens and yellows with pops of lavender, Vuillard achieved a remarkable range of textures and tonalities, from the sunlit tree bark to the velvety foliage deep in the shadows.

title: Two Sauceboats and Two Covered Tureens from the Washington Memorial Service
short_description: Chinese porcelain made especially for export to the United States often displays painted imagery of subjects, such as commemorative events, that appealed to wealthy American consumers. Part of a larger suite, these four pieces were commissioned around 1800 in remembrance of the nation’s first president, who died in 1799. Symbols such as the weeping willow, tomb, and eagle reflect the contemporary mourning for Washington.
